newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces hard week at home after summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces hard week at home after summit.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin faces a battle on two fronts this week, completing a liberal overhaul of his government and tackling protest strikes across the sprawling federation.

Trade unions, exasperated by government failure to pay wages, have called strikes for March 27. The action, which must ring alarm bells in the Kremlin at a time when it is seeking to rein in spending, is backed by Yeltsin's chief foe, the communist party.

But the two new leading lights in the government, first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, made clear over the weekend that, like Yeltsin, they were fighting fit and ready to press on with the next stage of reform.
"We know what has to be done. We know that a big part of this job is far from being attractive," Chubais, 41, told Public Russian Television (ORT) on Saturday night.
"But we are taking it on will full clarity and open eyes."

Yeltsin, back at the helm of power firmly after eight months of illness, launched a government reshuffle last week which brought a team of youthful reformers to the top cabinet positions, first of all Chubais and Nemtsov, who is 37.
The most important decisions announced, he attended a summit with President Bill Clinton in Helsinki at the end of the week, re-establishing himself on the international scene.

The prime tasks of the cabinet, headed by veteran prime minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, is to break a vicious circle of tax dodging and a huge backlog in pensions and salaries. At the same time he must fight corruption and organised crime which the president says challenges the state itself.

Nemtsov, also speaking on ORT, said he shared Yeltsin's desire to make Russia "not a bandit, corrupt country". He wanted to bring in "popular, democratic capitalism" instead of "corrupt state capitalism".

He said he realised his job would lead to a clash with an industrial and financial oligarchy. "You can imagine the fuss which will start when it comes to concrete interests of concrete financial groups," he said.

The distribution of powers between the two first deputy prime ministers and six deputies to Chernomyrdin is yet to be announced, as well as more new ministerial appointments but Chubais indicated he had already scored a major victory.

He said control over customs service, tax inspection and police, and currency control would be concentrated in the hands of his ally, Alfred Kokh, who combines the post of privatisation minister with the duties of deputy premier.
Up to now tax and customs services were in the hands of the more conservative Anatoly Kulikov, Interior Minister and Deputy Prime Minister.

Yeltsin, with his vast constitutional powers, can easily afford to ignore criticism by the communist-led opposition which call results of his summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton a sell-out over NATO's expansion plans.

But a tougher test for Yeltsin and the government would be on Thursday, when the trade unions plan a day of action to protest against chronic delays in payment of wages and pensions across the vast federation.

The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament has effectively backed the trade unions and the Communist Party, the best-organised single political force in the country, is using its grass root bodies to back the protest.
Chubais travelled to the coal mining region of Kuzbass last week trying to defuse the tension in one of the potentionally most explosive regions and appeared to have some success.
But the authorities are still clearly alarmed.
Eduard Rossel, governor of the industrial Urals region of Yekaterinburg, told ORT he had never been so worried.

Chernomyrdin has asked regional leaders, who form the Federation Council upper chamber, to stay in their home towns to help keep a lid on tensions and a session of the Council planned for this week has been postponed.

Chernomyrdin urged regional leaders to make extra efforts to pay off wage arrears and also ordered a beefing up of security arrangements to preempt social unrest, Interfax news agency said. "We must not allow any provocations," Chernomyrdin said.
